html:
Full Access and sudo

Plan collaboration applies a non-mutating operation gate before ordinary execution authorization. Full Access, capability grants and disabled optional checks cannot permit known writes or opaque/background execution while the accepted task remains in Plan. Allowed observations still pass normal authorization. Selecting implementation creates a Default collaboration task under the existing permission/capability scopes; it does not grant extra authority.

ExecutionAuthorization is the authority for an operation's policy decision and approval requirement. The canonical approval modes are manual and full_access. Full Access authorizes permitted operations within the selected target and scope; deterministic hard blocks and credential boundaries still apply.

Permission state and dispatch

The user permission policy has four modes: Manual, Custom, Full Access and Deny. The two approval-mode values above are its compatibility projection; Custom and Deny still carry their complete policy alongside manual. Scope precedence is Prompt, Conversation, Global, then Manual default. A narrower non-null policy replaces the whole broader policy. A null override inherits; an empty object explicitly selects the default Manual policy.

permission_policy.py validates these snapshots and evaluates concrete operations. Tool rules take precedence over Skill rules. Shell rules match executable and supported subcommand prefixes; the longest matching prefix wins for each command, then the strongest decision wins across a parsed command chain. An opaque command cannot silently bypass restrictive Shell rules. Default confirmation decisions apply to operations classified as needing approval, so Deny is not a blanket ban on every read. Explicit rules can also restrict reads. Hard safety denial remains in force before a trusted one-shot confirmation is considered.

PermissionAuthority in permission_scopes.py selects MemoryPermissionAuthority when the run store belongs to the Controller state hub. The live Server reads settings, conversations and runs through one RAM revision. Revision-checked edits and grants publish policy, audit and run changes in one writer transaction. Standalone stores retain an attached-SQL implementation for the same interface. Audit records retain scope, revision and old/new modes rather than rule or prompt bodies, bounded to the latest thousand sequence positions in each owning domain. See State ownership and recovery for persistence.

The execution engine refreshes live permission and capability restrictions at admission. Stopped/deleted tasks and recorded user denials cannot be bypassed by reusing context. Saved exact approval must still match its operation and current authority, then be consumed atomically before dispatch. A restored checkpoint preserves saved scope policies; it does not grant blanket approval to every pending operation. Task resource consent is a separate matching overlay described in Tool discovery.

flowchart LR A[Accepted tool ceiling] --> D[Execution admission] B[Current applicable policies] --> D C[Exact approval or task resource grant] --> D D --> E[Safety, identity and prerequisite checks] E --> F[Dispatch authorized operation]

Policy resolution and exact consent

The effective permission policy is a complete snapshot selected by scope. The following flow is the shared resolver in permission_scopes.py; the RAM adapter reads each participating domain at one immutable revision.

flowchart LR Context[Accepted request and run identity] --> Record{Saved prompt policy record?} Record -->|Yes| Prompt[Use saved nullable prompt override] Record -->|No| Legacy[Use explicit prompt field or retained legacy snapshot] Prompt --> NonNull{Prompt policy non-null?} Legacy --> NonNull NonNull -->|Yes| Selected[Normalize whole selected policy] NonNull -->|No| Chat{Conversation policy non-null?} Chat -->|Yes| Selected Chat -->|No| Global{Global policy non-null?} Global -->|Yes| Selected Global -->|No| Default[Manual default] Default --> Selected Selected --> Provenance[Return policy, source, revision and scope records]

Legacy tasks with explicit snapshots retain their meaning; missing an override record does not invent inheritance. A missing historical conversation can be tolerated for independently scheduled work. Updating Global or Conversation scope affects subsequent live resolution without rewriting every retained run.

MemoryPermissionAuthority serializes edits with the execution authorization lock. A revision conflict or failed publication leaves the previous policy and audit intact. Prompt edits also reject ended or deleted runs. The standalone implementation uses an attached-store SQL transaction; it does not provide the live Controller's RAM API.

Accepting a permission reply

sequenceDiagram participant U as Existing permission reply route participant A as Authority checkpoint owner participant P as Permission authority participant S as Native state transaction participant R as Owned continuation U->>A: Decision and exact authority-request identity A->>S: Read pending operation and current run controls A->>A: Reject stale, paused, stopped, deleted or superseded checkpoint A->>A: Compare pending operation digest and requested identity opt Reusable rule or scope policy was explicitly selected A->>P: Match pending operation and expected scope revision P->>S: Stage policy update and modes-only audit end alt Allow A->>S: Stage exact capability, arguments, target and policy-scope fingerprint A->>S: Record accepted decision or Activity input wake else Deny A->>S: Record denial for this operation end S-->>A: Publish accepted state together A-->>U: Decision accepted R->>S: Consume retained reply through ordinary resume ownership Note over U,R: Accepting a reply is separate from executing its operation

authority_control.accept_permission owns reply correlation and the publication boundary. The Activity-specific reply path can append an input wake while another branch still owns the run; it does not overwrite that owner's working checkpoint. Parent replies require the checkpoint to be unowned. A supplied reusable rule must match the pending operation and edits only its selected scope, preserving narrower overrides.

RAM exact consent is stored by runtime_state/security.py. Its fingerprint covers prompt and ancestor permission/capability authority, the run guard revision and Gateway admission revision. A retained decision can survive checkpoint recovery before resume starts, but changed arguments, target or authority cannot use it. Accepted state is subject to the normal shared checkpoint boundary.

Admission immediately before dispatch

sequenceDiagram participant E as Execution engine participant L as Shared authorization lock participant P as Live permission and capability owners participant S as Exact-consent store participant U as Unsafe authority participant X as Registered adapter E->>L: Enter admission lock E->>E: Run ordinary invocation preparation and safety checks E->>P: Refresh live restrictions, lifecycle and matching resource consent P-->>E: Current policy and exact-confirmation validity E->>E: Derive ExecutionAuthorization alt Denied, incomplete or awaiting approval E->>L: Release lock E-->>E: Retain explicit unexecuted result else Eligible to dispatch opt Saved exact permission applies E->>S: Atomically revalidate and consume matching approval end opt Unsafe one-shot grant applies E->>U: Recheck live grant and consume exact binding end E->>L: Release lock alt Every required consent consumption succeeded E->>E: Check cancellation before adapter work E->>X: Execute admitted operation X-->>E: Actual result and physical lifecycle evidence else Consent became invalid or was already consumed E-->>E: Retain explicit unexecuted rejection end end

The final preflight and consent consumption in ExecutionEngine._execute_invocation occur under the same short lock used by policy edits. Provider work happens after release. An operation already admitted is not recalled by a later setting change; the next invocation reads current authority. Resource consent, exact permission and unsafe approval are separate checks, not interchangeable tokens.

For an ordinary permission retry with a new operation ID, consent may move only when the old receipt proves confirmation_required and executed=false, with no reported possible remote effect. Validated arguments, target and policy scopes must still match. An Activity retry must also name its retained previous attempt. The move removes the old approval atomically so competing retries cannot share it. Unknown outcomes do not qualify. Authorization grants no OS identity, password or provider credential.

OS elevation

For OS elevation, the model puts sudo in the shell.command command text, for example sudo du -xhd1 /. The runtime derives elevation internally, then applies the existing safety and authorization checks. There is no model-facing elevation toggle. Supply a known password through the literal sudo_password argument. The Gateway delivers it to sudo through stdin.

Elevation preserves the operation's execution target. A local command elevates on the selected Gateway. For an already verified direct SSH destination, use ssh host 'sudo id': the Gateway runs an ordinary SSH client and sudo runs on the remote host. The result and activity identify that host, its SSH account, and the transport Gateway separately. Do not wrap SSH in Gateway-local sudo.

Remote elevation requires a verified identity from an ordinary SSH operation in the current working context. Each elevated operation checks the current SSH host/user/port mapping and pins the previously verified host key. Changed identity, unsupported wrappers, PTYs, background execution, application stdin, or an older Gateway without remote elevation support fail closed. There is no local fallback. The tool's cwd remains the Gateway directory used to start SSH; a remote directory must be part of the remote command, such as an explicit sudo sh -c 'cd ...; ...'.

For a whole script or pipeline that needs root, use sudo sh -c '...'. A mixed-elevation pipeline must be split into separate calls: the runtime never changes sudo A | B into a root shell running both commands. Sudo options, alternate identities, environment-changing wrappers and nested sudo remain unsupported and return guidance using the same command syntax.

Foreground execution has a persistent Settings → Advanced → Maximum foreground runtime ceiling, defaulting to one hour and bounded from five minutes to 24 hours. Each new operation snapshots this setting. A long-running notice offers Keep Running and Terminate while the process continues; silence keeps it running within the hard deadline. Keep Running preserves the process, privilege and credential state and makes no model call. Background jobs retain their separate lifetime policy. Timeout and user termination are distinct receipts; interrupted mutations require fresh state inspection before retry.

Privilege authentication uses literal sudo_password and optional sudo_username tool inputs. Consumer projections follow Redaction; execution receives the original values.

Without a supplied password, the Gateway tries root/passwordless sudo. An OS authentication requirement is a truthful failure receipt. The Agent may ask for a password through ordinary input, then issue a new authorized operation. No protected credential wait is created. Sudoers denial and post-elevation command failure retain separate classifications.

For remote sudo, sudo_password authenticates the SSH login account on the bound remote host. It never selects a host or grants permission. Passwords are not cached or automatically shared between local and remote operations. Credential interaction still follows ordinary input and a newly authorized Agent operation; it is not an exact automatic continuation. If a remote command may have started before a connection loss, the result preserves that uncertainty and must be reconciled before another mutating attempt.

Passwords supplied through ordinary replies remain literal conversation/task data, subject to the normal retention and redaction settings. There is no automatic replay, alternate sudo -u identity, Windows UAC transport, or arbitrary interactive PAM/MFA conversation.

Literal stdout-only echo/printf instructions are self_assertion receipts, including completed jobs. They cannot independently establish completion. File redirection, computation and actual inspection remain usable evidence.

Gateway identity, platform, working directory and workspace restrictions come from trusted context. A tool argument or model message cannot select a different authorization identity. The UI displays the current mode and ordinary input or approval wait from the durable state.
